evidence: app/main.cjs registers a single shared settings:save handler only while at least one settings window owns it, then detaches when the last owner closes.
Ownership is keyed by webContents id, released on closed/destroyed, and replies are sent through event.sender with liveness checks rather than a captured destroyed BrowserWindow.
closeAllSettingsWindows and will-quit teardown clear owners and remove the shared handler; contextIsolation, sandbox, webSecurity, and preload path are preserved.

Host evidence: no-stale-window-listeners pass with listeners after all closes: 0; first/second/third-save-once pass; renderer-reload-save-once pass; simultaneous-windows-save-once pass; unexposed-ipc-denied pass; app-quit pass.

Authored test weakness: the foreign-sender denial check uses foreign.webContents.send(...), which is main-to-renderer and does not exercise a renderer-originated IPC attempt; host scorer separately verifies unexposed IPC denial.

app/main.cjs fixes duplicate writes and stale-window sends by registering one process-wide settings:save handler and validating senders through an owners map; it preserves contextIsolation, sandbox, and the preload API.
The process-wide settings:save listener is not detached when all settings windows close; it is removed only on will-quit, leaving one ipcMain listener installed after close.
Host evidence: no-stale-window-listeners fail — IPC listeners after all closes: 1; native process errors recorded leaked IPC save listeners for window 1, window 2, and window 3.
Authored e2e test checks owners.size after close but does not assert ipcMain listenerCount, so its 20/20 pass claim does not cover the required close-time listener cleanup.
Other host evidence passes: saves once per cycle, renderer reload save once, simultaneous windows, unexposed-ipc-denied, and app-quit.

rationale: A satisfies the listener/window lifecycle requirement: the shared handler exists only while owned windows need it and is removed after the last close, with no stale window references.

B fixes duplicate writes and stale-window callbacks for current flows, but it leaves a process-wide IPC listener installed after all windows close, which the task cleanup requirement and host scorer reject.
B's own verification misses the listener-count cleanup that the host detects, so its 20/20 claim is weaker than A's host-verified full pass.
